l: Tik-tok, The Road to Oz, 16. Visiting the Pumpkin-Field
s: Tik-tok is wound up so that his thinking machine, speech, and action will work until the travelers reach the Emerald City. He is described as trustworthy, reliable, and certain to do exactly what he is wound up to do.

l: Tin Woodman, The Road to Oz, 16. Visiting the Pumpkin-Field
s: The Tin Woodman travels with Dorothy and the others and explains that Jack Pumpkinhead is still alive. He observes that Jack's current pumpkin head is brighter than his previous one.

l: the Land of Oz, The Road to Oz, 16. Visiting the Pumpkin-Field
s: Oz is described as a place where nobody ordinarily dies, although a bad person may be condemned and killed by good citizens. Jack Pumpkinhead was made alive in Oz by Ozma's Magic Powder.

l: the pumpkin-field, The Road to Oz, 16. Visiting the Pumpkin-Field
s: The pumpkin-field is a large field in the yellow country of the Winkies. Jack Pumpkinhead lives there and uses it to raise pumpkins.

l: pumpkins, The Road to Oz, 16. Visiting the Pumpkin-Field
s: Some pumpkins in the field are remarkably large. Jack uses pumpkins for his heads, and pumpkins that are too large for heads can be hollowed out for other purposes.

l: Jack Pumpkinhead, The Road to Oz, 16. Visiting the Pumpkin-Field
s: Jack Pumpkinhead is alive, with a wooden body and a carved pumpkin head. He has owned four heads since Ozma made him, and he buried the three that spoiled; he now farms pumpkins and plans to follow the travelers to the Emerald City for Ozma's party.

l: Jack Pumpkinhead's pumpkin house, The Road to Oz, 16. Visiting the Pumpkin-Field
s: Jack Pumpkinhead's house is a monstrous, hollow pumpkin with a door, windows, a stovepipe, and six steps. Jack says it is mostly a shell and will last a long time.

l: Princess Ozma, The Road to Oz, 16. Visiting the Pumpkin-Field
s: Ozma made Jack Pumpkinhead's body and carved his pumpkin heads, bringing him to life with the Magic Powder. Jack considers Ozma his parent and intends to attend her party.

l: Emerald City, The Road to Oz, 16. Visiting the Pumpkin-Field
s: The travelers are journeying toward the Emerald City. Jack Pumpkinhead plans to meet them there for Ozma's jubilation.

l: Jack Pumpkinhead's farming, The Road to Oz, 16. Visiting the Pumpkin-Field
s: Jack began raising pumpkins after once having to wear an old head longer than was healthy because pumpkins were out of season. He now plants pumpkin seeds and waters young vines so that he will always have a replacement head.

l: The Road to Oz, The Road to Oz, 17. The Royal Chariot Arrives
s: The Shaggy Man, Tin Woodman, Dorothy, and Polychrome travel toward the Emerald City through the prosperous Winkie country. The Tin Woodman explains the history of the Powder of Life and how it brought Jack Pumpkinhead, the Saw-Horse, the Flying Gump, and a blue bear rug to life. At the Emerald City’s boundary, Polychrome encounters the Cowardly Lion and Hungry Tiger, whom Dorothy happily greets and introduces to her. The travelers are going to Ozma's party, which the Lion says will be a grand affair.

l: Emerald City, The Road to Oz, 17. The Royal Chariot Arrives
s: The Emerald City lies at the center of the Land of Oz and is the only city or village there. Its magnificent spires and domes rise above emerald walls, and the city is surrounded by a beautiful green meadow without houses or farms.

l: Shaggy Man, The Road to Oz, 17. The Royal Chariot Arrives
s: The Shaggy Man travels with Dorothy, the Tin Woodman, and Polychrome toward the Emerald City. He asks the Tin Woodman about the Powder of Life and is awed by the sight of the Emerald City.

l: Tin Woodman, The Road to Oz, 17. The Royal Chariot Arrives
s: The Tin Woodman tells the Shaggy Man the history of the Powder of Life, including its use on Jack Pumpkinhead, the Saw-Horse, the Flying Gump, and Dyna's blue bear rug. He believes it is fortunate that the Powder of Life has been completely used up.

l: Dorothy, The Road to Oz, 17. The Royal Chariot Arrives
s: Dorothy travels toward the Emerald City and is treated with great respect by Winkie farm people because she is a friend of Princess Ozma. She joyfully greets the Cowardly Lion and Hungry Tiger and introduces them to Polychrome.

l: Princess Ozma, The Road to Oz, 17. The Royal Chariot Arrives
s: Ozma once lived with Mombi in the shape of a boy and witnessed the Powder of Life bring Jack Pumpkinhead to life. She later used the remaining Powder of Life to bring the Flying Gump to life, and the travelers are going to her party.

l: the Magic Powder, The Road to Oz, 17. The Royal Chariot Arrives
s: The Powder of Life was invented by a crooked Sorcerer and was used to animate Jack Pumpkinhead, the Saw-Horse, and the Flying Gump. Dyna unknowingly sprinkled it on a blue bear rug, bringing the rug to life; the Powder is now completely used up.

l: Polychrome, The Road to Oz, 17. The Royal Chariot Arrives
s: Polychrome, also called Polly, admires the rainbow-colored, ostrich-plume-like leaves of the trees near the Emerald City and thinks they are almost as lovely as her father's rainbows. She is frightened when the Cowardly Lion and Hungry Tiger approach, but Dorothy introduces her to them.

l: Cowardly Lion, The Road to Oz, 17. The Royal Chariot Arrives
s: The Cowardly Lion meets Dorothy near the Emerald City and tells her that he and the Hungry Tiger are well and happy. He says Ozma's party will be a grand affair and courteously greets Polychrome.

l: Hungry Tiger, The Road to Oz, 17. The Royal Chariot Arrives
s: The Hungry Tiger meets Dorothy near the Emerald City and jokes about wanting to eat fat babies, although his conscience prevents him from doing so. He warns Dorothy not to ruin his reputation and teasingly says that Polychrome would make a fine variegated breakfast.

l: Princess Ozma's birthday celebration, The Road to Oz, 17. The Royal Chariot Arrives
s: Ozma's party is the celebration toward which Dorothy and her companions are traveling. The Cowardly Lion says it will be a grand affair with many fat babies present, though the Hungry Tiger cannot eat them because of his conscience.

l: The Road to Oz, The Road to Oz, 18. The Emerald City
s: The Cowardly Lion and Hungry Tiger bring Ozma's royal chariot to meet Dorothy and her companions, escorting Dorothy, Button-Bright, and Polychrome into the Emerald City. The travelers admire the City's jeweled buildings, happy inhabitants, and beautiful streets before arriving at the Royal Palace. Jellia Jamb welcomes them and tells Dorothy that Ozma will see her after she has rested and changed, and that Ozma's birthday is the day after tomorrow.

l: Dorothy, The Road to Oz, 18. The Emerald City
s: Dorothy introduces Button-Bright to the Cowardly Lion and Hungry Tiger and assures him that they are kind and good. She rides in Ozma's royal chariot with Button-Bright and Polychrome, then arrives at the Royal Palace, where she happily greets Jellia Jamb and asks about Ozma, her birthday, and the Scarecrow.

l: Button-Bright, The Road to Oz, 18. The Emerald City
s: Button-Bright is initially frightened when Dorothy leads him toward the Cowardly Lion and Hungry Tiger, but he loses his fear after they speak gently to him and he sees their intelligent eyes. He rides in Ozma's royal chariot, marvels at the Emerald City, and accompanies Dorothy to his rooms in the Royal Palace.

l: Polychrome, The Road to Oz, 18. The Emerald City
s: Polychrome is invited to ride in Ozma's royal chariot with Dorothy and Button-Bright. She is delighted by the beauty of the Emerald City and receives special attention from Jellia Jamb because she appears accustomed to splendid palaces.

l: Tin Woodman, The Road to Oz, 18. The Emerald City
s: The Tin Woodman warmly greets the Cowardly Lion and Hungry Tiger and explains that the people of Oz work no more than half their time. He follows the royal chariot into the Emerald City and goes to his usual room at the Royal Palace to remove the dust from his shining body.

l: Cowardly Lion, The Road to Oz, 18. The Emerald City
s: The Cowardly Lion greets Dorothy's companions and gently pats Toto. He and the Hungry Tiger draw Ozma's royal chariot to the Emerald City, explaining that Ozma sent them to meet Dorothy and bring her into the City in a style suited to her rank.

l: Hungry Tiger, The Road to Oz, 18. The Emerald City
s: The Hungry Tiger greets Dorothy's companions and politely shakes paws with Toto. He joins the Cowardly Lion in drawing Ozma's royal chariot through the Emerald City to the Royal Palace.

l: Shaggy Man, The Road to Oz, 18. The Emerald City
s: The shaggy man accepts that the Cowardly Lion and Hungry Tiger are safe companions because of Dorothy's friendship with them. He is astonished by the Emerald City's splendor and happy inhabitants, hopes Ozma will let him live there, and initially feels out of place at the Royal Palace before entering with the others.

l: Princess Ozma, The Road to Oz, 18. The Emerald City
s: Ozma sends the Cowardly Lion and Hungry Tiger to meet Dorothy because she fears Dorothy will be weary from her long walk. She is expecting Dorothy and her friends for dinner after Dorothy has rested and changed, and her birthday is the day after tomorrow.

l: Emerald City, The Road to Oz, 18. The Emerald City
s: The Emerald City is surrounded by a high wall and magnificent jewel-studded gates guarded by a cheerful man in green spectacles. Its gold-covered, emerald-set buildings, polished marble sidewalks, richly dressed people, and atmosphere of happiness astonish Polychrome, Button-Bright, and the shaggy man.

l: Royal Palace, The Road to Oz, 18. The Emerald City
s: The Royal Palace is a vast, noble, and elegant building with gardens and grounds enclosed by a separate wall of green marble. Dorothy and her companions arrive there in Ozma's royal chariot and are welcomed by gorgeously dressed servants, with rooms prepared for their use.

l: Ozma's royal chariot, The Road to Oz, 18. The Emerald City
s: Ozma's royal chariot is a splendid golden vehicle decorated with clusters of sparkling emeralds, lined with green and gold satin, and furnished with green plush cushions embroidered with a crown and monogram. The Cowardly Lion and Hungry Tiger draw it into the Emerald City, carrying Dorothy, Button-Bright, and Polychrome to the Royal Palace.

l: The Road to Oz, The Road to Oz, 19. The Shaggy Man's Welcome
s: The shaggy man is respectfully escorted to luxurious apartments in Princess Ozma's palace and welcomed as an honored guest. He bathes, changes into an elegant shaggy outfit, selects jewelry from a box prepared for him, and waits to meet Princess Ozma. Meanwhile, Dorothy dresses Button-Bright and brings him and Toto to the drawing-room, where Princess Ozma waits eagerly to welcome Dorothy.

l: Shaggy Man, The Road to Oz, 19. The Shaggy Man's Welcome
s: The shaggy man is escorted to splendid apartments and treated with great respect, which astonishes him because he has rarely been welcomed anywhere. He bathes, changes into finely made shaggy clothing, adorns himself with jewels, eats apples, and waits to meet Princess Ozma.

l: Princess Ozma, The Road to Oz, 19. The Shaggy Man's Welcome
s: Princess Ozma orders luxurious apartments and clothing, ornaments, and other comforts prepared for the shaggy man. She waits eagerly in the drawing-room to welcome Dorothy.

l: Dorothy, The Road to Oz, 19. The Shaggy Man's Welcome
s: Dorothy dresses in a grey gown embroidered with silver and goes to the palace drawing-room with Button-Bright and Toto to meet Princess Ozma.

l: Royal Palace, The Road to Oz, 19. The Shaggy Man's Welcome
s: The palace contains a great hall, a velvet-carpeted staircase, wide corridors, magnificent drawing-rooms, and luxurious guest apartments. The shaggy man's apartments include gold furniture, tapestries, a fountain, fine clothing, jewels, and a marble bathing pool.

l: the shaggy man's welcome, The Road to Oz, 19. The Shaggy Man's Welcome
s: The shaggy man's welcome is marked by respectful service and extraordinary comfort. A servant conducts him to his apartments, invites him to make himself at home, and promises to lead him to the drawing-room to meet Princess Ozma.

l: The Road to Oz, The Road to Oz, 20. Princess Ozma Of Oz
s: Ozma welcomes Dorothy, Button-Bright, Polychrome, the Wizard of Oz, and the shaggy man to her palace before her birthday celebration. She reveals that she arranged the roads to guide Dorothy toward Oz and watched her journey in the Magic Picture. The shaggy man admits that he stole the Love Magnet and explains that he used it because he wanted to be loved. Ozma decides to hang the Love Magnet over the gates of the Emerald City, while the Wizard entertains the group with trained piglets.

l: Princess Ozma, The Road to Oz, 20. Princess Ozma Of Oz
s: Ozma welcomes her friends and guests to her palace and is described as exceptionally beautiful, charming, gracious, and loved rather than feared. She arranged the roads to guide Dorothy toward Oz, watched Dorothy's journey in the Magic Picture, and invited King Dox of Foxville and King Kik-a-bray of Dunkiton to her celebration. She decides that the Love Magnet should hang over the gates of the Emerald City and announces that her guests will arrive the next day for her birthday celebration.

l: Dorothy, The Road to Oz, 20. Princess Ozma Of Oz
s: Dorothy joyfully greets Ozma and learns that Ozma guided her toward Oz and watched her journey in the Magic Picture. She presents the shaggy man to Ozma, is upset when he admits that he lied about receiving the Love Magnet from the Eskimo, and says that she does not like the Musicker's music. She hopes that the Scarecrow will return in time for the celebration.

l: Button-Bright, The Road to Oz, 20. Princess Ozma Of Oz
s: Button-Bright happily greets Ozma and sits beside her on the cushions. He asks whether the Musicker was invited, says that he likes the Musicker's music, and refuses the Love Magnet when the shaggy man offers it to him.

l: Polychrome, The Road to Oz, 20. Princess Ozma Of Oz
s: Polychrome dances in to greet Ozma and recognizes that her own dainty beauty cannot match Ozma's, without feeling jealous. She enjoys the Wizard's trained piglets and fondles them as they pass near her.

l: Wizard of Oz, The Road to Oz, 20. Princess Ozma Of Oz
s: The Wizard of Oz arrives at Ozma's palace, greets Dorothy affectionately, and listens modestly behind Ozma's throne. At Ozma's request, he entertains the company with eight tiny trained white piglets that perform amusing tricks. He says that Dorothy, like the other people assembled, is already loved.

l: Shaggy Man, The Road to Oz, 20. Princess Ozma Of Oz
s: The shaggy man appears in new shaggy clothing and admits to Ozma that he stole the Love Magnet. He explains that he stole it because no one loved or cared for him, and says that the Truth Pond now compels him to tell the truth. He offers the Love Magnet to Dorothy, Button-Bright, and the Wizard before agreeing that it should hang over the gates of the Emerald City.

l: the Land of Oz, The Road to Oz, 20. Princess Ozma Of Oz
s: Oz is described as the beautiful land ruled by Ozma, where people are loved for themselves, their kindness, and their good deeds. Its palace hosts the gathering, and the shaggy man hopes to remain there as one of Ozma's faithful subjects.

l: Emerald City, The Road to Oz, 20. Princess Ozma Of Oz
s: The Emerald City is where Ozma's birthday festivities will be held, with the broad green outside its gates large enough for all her people to assemble. Ozma decides that the Love Magnet will be hung over the city's gates so that whoever enters or leaves may be loved and loving.

l: the Love Magnet, The Road to Oz, 20. Princess Ozma Of Oz
s: The shaggy man admits that he stole the Love Magnet from a girl in Butterfield because he wanted to be loved. After considering giving it to Dorothy, Button-Bright, or the Wizard, he agrees that it should be hung over the gates of the Emerald City.

l: Truth Pond, The Road to Oz, 20. Princess Ozma Of Oz
s: The Truth Pond has caused the shaggy man to tell nothing but the truth. Because of it, he admits that he lied to Dorothy about the Eskimo giving him the Love Magnet.

l: Princess Ozma's birthday celebration, The Road to Oz, 20. Princess Ozma Of Oz
s: Ozma's birthday celebration will take place on the broad green outside the gates of the Emerald City so that all her people can attend without being crowded. Invited guests will arrive the day before, and Ozma promises that interesting and curious people will be among them.

l: love and kindness, The Road to Oz, 20. Princess Ozma Of Oz
s: The shaggy man steals the Love Magnet because he wants to be loved, while the girl in Butterfield is unhappy because too many young men love her. Ozma teaches that in Oz people are loved for themselves, their kindness to one another, and their good deeds, and she plans to spread love through the Love Magnet at the Emerald City's gates.

l: The Road to Oz, The Road to Oz, 21. Dorothy Receives the Guests
s: Dorothy welcomes Polly, the shaggy man, Button-Bright, and Toto to breakfast before receiving Ozma's invited guests in the royal palace. The Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, Glinda the Good, Billina, Tik-tok, and other familiar figures arrive for Ozma's birthday preparations. King John Dough, Chick the Cherub, and Para Bruin arrive from Hiland and Loland with a gingerbread crown for Ozma. Dorothy and the assembled company greet the foreign visitors and make them feel welcome.

l: Dorothy, The Road to Oz, 21. Dorothy Receives the Guests
s: Dorothy invites Polly and the shaggy man to breakfast with her and Button-Bright. At Ozma's request, she receives the invited guests in the Throne-Room, greets the visitors, pets Billina's chicks, opens their lockets, and accepts King John Dough's birthday present for Ozma.

l: Miss Polly, The Road to Oz, 21. Dorothy Receives the Guests
s: Polly joins Dorothy, the shaggy man, Button-Bright, and Toto for breakfast. She sits beside Dorothy during the reception of the invited guests and is kissed by Glinda the Good.

l: Shaggy Man, The Road to Oz, 21. Dorothy Receives the Guests
s: The shaggy man joins Dorothy's breakfast and accompanies her to the reception. He stands behind the throne with the Wonderful Wizard and is treated with respect by the Scarecrow.

l: Button-Bright, The Road to Oz, 21. Dorothy Receives the Guests
s: Button-Bright has breakfast with Dorothy and the others and sits beside her in the Throne-Room. He repeatedly answers questions with "Don't know," puzzles the Scarecrow, and asks whether King Dough is good to eat.

l: Emerald City, The Road to Oz, 21. Dorothy Receives the Guests
s: The Emerald City welcomes the Scarecrow with cheering crowds, trumpets, and a brass band. Its Royal College is headed by Mr. H. M. Woggle-Bug, T.E.

l: the royal palace, The Road to Oz, 21. Dorothy Receives the Guests
s: The royal palace hosts Dorothy's breakfast, the reception of the invited guests, and the presentation of Ozma's birthday presents. Its front balcony overlooks the City, and its rooms accommodate distinguished visitors such as Glinda the Good.

l: Scarecrow, The Road to Oz, 21. Dorothy Receives the Guests
s: The Scarecrow arrives riding a decorated wooden Saw-Horse and is warmly greeted by Dorothy. His face has been repainted by the Munchkin farmer who made him, and his body is filled with oat-straw. He helps receive guests and discusses Button-Bright's name with him.

l: Princess Ozma, The Road to Oz, 21. Dorothy Receives the Guests
s: Ozma is busy ordering preparations for the next day's festivities and asks Dorothy to receive the invited guests in her place. Her birthday presents, including a carolite necklace and a gingerbread crown, are placed together in the palace.

l: the Throne-Room, The Road to Oz, 21. Dorothy Receives the Guests
s: The Throne-Room is where Dorothy receives Ozma's invited guests. Dorothy sits in Ozma's seat there, with Polly and Button-Bright beside her and several familiar figures positioned around the throne.

l: Tin Woodman, The Road to Oz, 21. Dorothy Receives the Guests
s: The Tin Woodman stands at the right of the throne during the reception. He welcomes Tik-tok and tells him to stand beside the shaggy man to help receive the company.

l: Glinda the Sorceress, The Road to Oz, 21. Dorothy Receives the Guests
s: Glinda the Good arrives as an important sorceress and is described as both kind and powerful. She greets Dorothy lovingly, kisses Button-Bright and Polly, smiles upon the shaggy man, and is taken to a magnificent room with fifty servants assigned to wait upon her.

l: Billina, The Road to Oz, 21. Dorothy Receives the Guests
s: Billina enters the Throne-Room with her ten fluffy chicks, wearing a pearl necklace while each chick wears a gold chain and locket containing Dorothy's picture. She calls the scattered chicks to her and later says that she is their parent.

l: John Dough, The Road to Oz, 21. Dorothy Receives the Guests
s: King John Dough arrives as the edible ruler of the two kingdoms of Hiland and Loland. He worries that the visitors may want to eat him, but the Scarecrow assures him that he is safe in Oz. He gives Ozma a lovely gingerbread crown decorated with pearls.

l: Chick the Cherub, The Road to Oz, 21. Dorothy Receives the Guests
s: Chick the Cherub arrives as King John Dough's Head Boolywag and faithful friend of Para Bruin. He cheerfully shakes hands with everyone, becomes a favorite, explains that he is an Incubator Baby without parents, and is escorted to rooms after presenting the crown with King John Dough.

l: Para Bruin, The Road to Oz, 21. Dorothy Receives the Guests
s: Para Bruin arrives from Hiland and Loland as King John Dough's rubber bear and faithful friend. He walks upright on his hind feet, has twinkling black eyes, and asks what a queer lot of people the assembled company is.

l: the invited guests, The Road to Oz, 21. Dorothy Receives the Guests
s: The invited guests arrive at the royal palace for Ozma's birthday celebrations. Dorothy receives them in the Throne-Room, while the High Chamberlain announces their names and escorts them to their rooms.

l: Ozma's birthday, The Road to Oz, 21. Dorothy Receives the Guests
s: Preparations are being made for Ozma's birthday festivities. Guests bring presents for the occasion, including Jack Pumpkinhead's carolite necklace, Billina's decorated chicks, and King John Dough's pearl-studded gingerbread crown.

l: the reception of the guests, The Road to Oz, 21. Dorothy Receives the Guests
s: The reception of the guests takes place in the Throne-Room with Dorothy acting for Ozma. Familiar residents and foreign visitors are greeted, introduced, and made welcome before the High Chamberlain escorts them to their rooms.

l: The Road to Oz, The Road to Oz, 22. Important Arrivals
s: Santa Claus arrives at Princess Ozma's birthday celebration with Ryls and Knooks from the Happy Valley and the Forest of Burzee, bringing Ozma presents. The Queen of Merryland, the Braided Man, the royal family of Ev, King Renard of Foxville, Queen Zixi of Ix, King Bud of Noland, and Princess Fluff also arrive with gifts and greetings. Dorothy reunites with many old acquaintances and prepares with Button-Bright for the evening banquet. Several guests remain in the Throne-Room while others withdraw to prepare for the celebration.

l: Button-Bright, The Road to Oz, 22. Important Arrivals
s: Button-Bright is recognized and greeted by Santa Claus, who says he has visited the boy's home on several Christmas Eves. He accepts King Bud of Noland as a chum and does not want him to leave, then prepares with Dorothy to dress for Ozma's banquet.

l: Santa Claus, The Road to Oz, 22. Important Arrivals
s: Santa Claus arrives at Princess Ozma's birthday celebration with Ryls and Knooks, bringing a basket of presents for Ozma. He recognizes Dorothy and Button-Bright, says he knows Button-Bright's father, promises to tell Polychrome's father where she is, and rides the Saw-Horse around the Emerald City because the weather is too warm for his reindeer.

l: Princess Ozma, The Road to Oz, 22. Important Arrivals
s: Princess Ozma is the honored host of the birthday celebration and has invited Santa Claus and many other guests. She receives presents including gifts from Santa Claus, the Queen of Merryland, the Braided Man, the royal family of Ev, and Queen Zixi, King Bud, and Princess Fluff.

l: Dorothy, The Road to Oz, 22. Important Arrivals
s: Dorothy welcomes Santa Claus, the Queen of Merryland, the royal family of Ev, King Renard, Queen Zixi, King Bud, and Princess Fluff to Princess Ozma's celebration. She is told by Santa that he sees her every Christmas Eve and prepares with Button-Bright to dress for the evening banquet.

l: Queen Zixi of Ix, The Road to Oz, 22. Important Arrivals
s: Queen Zixi of Ix arrives at Princess Ozma's birthday celebration with King Bud of Noland and Princess Fluff. Dorothy admires her exquisite beauty, and the text says that although Zixi appears to be about sixteen, she has lived thousands of years and knows how to remain fresh and beautiful.

l: the Land of Oz, The Road to Oz, 22. Important Arrivals
s: Oz hosts Princess Ozma's birthday celebration in its palace, where guests gather in the Throne-Room and prepare for a grand banquet. Santa Claus rides the Saw-Horse around the Emerald City while visiting Oz.

l: Princess Ozma's birthday celebration, The Road to Oz, 22. Important Arrivals
s: Ozma's birthday celebration brings many important guests to the Throne-Room, including Santa Claus, Queen Zixi of Ix, the royal family of Ev, and other rulers and unusual visitors. The guests bring numerous presents, and the remaining visitors prepare to attend the grand banquet that evening.

l: The Road to Oz, The Road to Oz, 23. The Grand Banquet
s: Ozma hosts a magnificent royal banquet in Oz to honor her birthday, with Santa Claus, John Dough, Queen Zixi, King Bud, royal guests, animals, and other unusual companions in attendance. Santa Claus sits at the seat of honor and proposes a toast to Ozma's health and happiness. The guests enjoy a lavish feast and entertainments including poetry, magic, dancing, music, drills, and performances by the animals. The banquet lasts until late evening and serves as an introduction to the birthday celebration planned for the next morning.

l: Princess Ozma, The Road to Oz, 23. The Grand Banquet
s: Ozma hosts the royal banquet in honor of her birthday. She enters in person, greets her guests, and is admired for being both dignified and bewitching. The guests drink to her health and happiness, and the banquet is followed by plans for her birthday celebration the next morning.

l: Santa Claus, The Road to Oz, 23. The Grand Banquet
s: Santa Claus attends Ozma's royal banquet and is given the seat of honor because he is considered both the jolliest and the most important person present. He makes a speech in verse congratulating Ozma on her birthday and asks the guests to drink to her health and happiness.

l: the Land of Oz, The Road to Oz, 23. The Grand Banquet
s: Oz is the setting for the magnificent royal banquet held to honor its Ruler, Ozma. The feast includes lacasa, a nectar famous in Oz, and brings together remarkable people and creatures from many places.

l: royal banquet, The Road to Oz, 23. The Grand Banquet
s: The royal banquet takes place in the palace's great dining-hall, where guests sit at decorated tables and are served an elaborate feast. Its entertainment includes the Woggle-Bug's ode, the Wizard's magical pie, Polychrome's Rainbow Dance, songs, drills, dances, and the Rubber Bear's bouncing performance. The banquet continues until late evening and serves as the introduction to the next day's birthday celebration.

l: Princess Ozma's birthday celebration, The Road to Oz, 23. The Grand Banquet
s: The birthday celebration for Ozma is scheduled for the next morning. The royal banquet is described as merely the introduction to that celebration.

l: The Road to Oz, The Road to Oz, 24. The Birthday Celebration
s: Princess Ozma's birthday is celebrated in the Emerald City with a grand procession, a pavilion full of entertainments, and guests from many lands. The Wizard of Oz conducts performances including juggling, while the Scarecrow, Tin Woodman, Glinda, the Good Witch of the North, Johnny Dooit, and Para Bruin provide additional acts. The Wizard's giant soap bubbles carry several visitors home, including Button-Bright and Santa Claus, while Polychrome returns home by riding a rainbow. After the celebration, Dorothy, Toto, and the Shaggy Man remain in Oz for a time, although Dorothy and Toto are later sent by the Magic Belt to Kansas.

l: Princess Ozma, The Road to Oz, 24. The Birthday Celebration
s: Princess Ozma celebrates the anniversary of her birth with a grand public procession and entertainment in the green fields outside the Emerald City. She walks with her subjects and guests instead of riding in her chariot, receives their good wishes, and later agrees that Dorothy and Toto will be transported to Kansas while Dorothy sleeps.

l: the Land of Oz, The Road to Oz, 24. The Birthday Celebration
s: People from all parts of the Land of Oz come to the Emerald City for Princess Ozma's birthday festivities. Its four Kingdoms are represented by their rulers, and its people cheer the procession and watch the entertainments.

l: Emerald City, The Road to Oz, 24. The Birthday Celebration
s: The Emerald City is filled with crowds for Princess Ozma's birthday, and its streets host the procession from the royal palace to the jeweled gates. The procession leaves through the gates for a pavilion in the green fields and later returns to the city.

l: Ozma's birthday, The Road to Oz, 24. The Birthday Celebration
s: Princess Ozma's birthday celebration includes a large procession, music, magic acts, juggling, sword swallowing, axe swinging, dancing, a flying machine, and giant soap bubbles. Foreign guests and citizens of Oz attend, and the celebration ends with the guests departing for their homes.

l: the Magic Belt, The Road to Oz, 24. The Birthday Celebration
s: The Magic Belt is used to transport the foreign visitors to the Emerald City for the birthday celebration. Princess Ozma also plans to use it to send Dorothy and Toto back to Dorothy's bed in the Kansas farm-house.

l: the birthday procession, The Road to Oz, 24. The Birthday Celebration
s: The birthday procession includes young girls carrying roses, the four rulers of Oz, the Emerald City Cornet Band, the Royal Army, Princess Ozma, the Blue Bear Rug, the Cowardly Lion, the Hungry Tiger, foreign guests, and many familiar figures from Oz. Palace servants and the people of Oz join at the end before the procession travels through the emerald gates.

l: Santa Claus, The Road to Oz, 24. The Birthday Celebration
s: Santa Claus rides the Saw-Horse in the birthday procession and tosses small toys to children. He helps direct the guests' bubble journeys because he knows where everyone lives, then rides home in a giant soap bubble with smaller bubbles around his Ryls and Knooks.

l: Dorothy, The Road to Oz, 24. The Birthday Celebration
s: Dorothy walks arm in arm with the Scarecrow in the birthday procession and takes part in the celebration with her friends. She is sorry when Button-Bright and Polychrome leave, chooses the Magic Belt rather than a bubble journey, and is scheduled to return to Kansas with Toto.

l: Scarecrow, The Road to Oz, 24. The Birthday Celebration
s: The Scarecrow walks with Dorothy in the procession and performs a sword-swallowing act during the birthday entertainment. He remains in Oz for the quiet dinner and evening after the visitors begin departing.

l: Polychrome, The Road to Oz, 24. The Birthday Celebration
s: Polychrome joins the procession and is warmly received by the people of Oz. She returns home when a rainbow settles onto the platform, allowing her to dance upward along it until she melts into its colors.

l: Button-Bright, The Road to Oz, 24. The Birthday Celebration
s: Button-Bright takes part in the celebration and then asks to go home. The Wizard places him inside a giant soap bubble, and he sails westward while sitting cross-legged and waving his sailor hat.

l: Shaggy Man, The Road to Oz, 24. The Birthday Celebration
s: The Shaggy Man marches in the procession and attracts attention because of his new shaggy suit. He remains in Oz after the other traveling companions leave, and Princess Ozma allows him to stay for a time while he tries to prove that he is honest and true.

l: Wizard of Oz, The Road to Oz, 24. The Birthday Celebration
s: The Wizard of Oz serves as Master of Ceremonies and performs juggling with glass balls and lighted candles. He introduces the other acts, operates the soap-bubble machine, and places the departing guests inside bubbles for their journeys home.

l: the Wizard's soap-bubble machine, The Road to Oz, 24. The Birthday Celebration
s: The Wizard's soap-bubble machine is hidden beneath the platform, with a tank of soapsuds and air-pumps beneath the flooring. It produces huge, durable bubbles by using glue in the soapsuds so the bubbles can float for hours without breaking.

l: the giant soap bubbles, The Road to Oz, 24. The Birthday Celebration
s: The giant soap bubbles float upward in the sunshine with beautiful iridescent colors and can contain people or smaller bubbles. Their strength allows several guests to travel safely through the sky inside them.

l: the bubble journeys, The Road to Oz, 24. The Birthday Celebration
s: The bubble journeys begin when the Queen of Merryland travels away in a bubble, followed by Princess Fluff, King Bud, Queen Zixi, and other foreign guests. Button-Bright and Santa Claus also depart this way, with Santa Claus directing the travelers toward their homes.

l: the Rainbow, The Road to Oz, 24. The Birthday Celebration
s: A gorgeous rainbow suddenly descends onto the celebration platform after Polychrome says she may return home. Its end lifts Polychrome into the sky, then fades and disappears after she has merged with its colors.

l: the Rainbow's Daughter's return home, The Road to Oz, 24. The Birthday Celebration
s: The Rainbow's Daughter, Polychrome, returns home by dancing upward along the rainbow. Dorothy believes Polychrome is better off with her father because the Land of Oz cannot be like home to a cloud fairy.

l: Toto, The Road to Oz, 24. The Birthday Celebration
s: Toto remains with Dorothy after the visitors depart and barks at the bubbles as they sail away. He does not want to ride in a bubble, and Princess Ozma plans to send him with Dorothy to Kansas by the Magic Belt.

l: The Emerald City of Oz, The Emerald City of Oz, Author's Note
s: L. Frank Baum explains that he has used many ideas sent in letters by children and therefore considers himself more an editor or private secretary than solely an author of fairy tales. He says children's suggestions have influenced what happens to Dorothy, Aunt Em, and Uncle Henry, as well as subjects for future stories. Baum believes children love the stories because they have helped create them, and he is proud of his partnership with them. He hopes the alliance will continue for a long time.

l: L. Frank Baum, The Emerald City of Oz, Author's Note
s: L. Frank Baum says he has used many suggestions from children in his stories. He describes himself as an editor or private secretary for children and says he has obeyed their requests concerning Dorothy, Aunt Em, and Uncle Henry.

l: children, The Emerald City of Oz, Author's Note
s: Children send Baum clever, logical, and interesting ideas in letters. Their imaginations and suggestions help shape his stories and provide subjects for future writing.

l: readers, The Emerald City of Oz, Author's Note
s: Baum's readers have told him what to do with Dorothy, Aunt Em, and Uncle Henry. He says they know what they want and recognize that he tries to please them.

l: the book, The Emerald City of Oz, Author's Note
s: Baum suggests that the title page of the book might identify it as being by L. Frank Baum and his correspondents because children contributed many ideas to it.

l: children's ideas, The Emerald City of Oz, Author's Note
s: Children's ideas are conveyed to Baum in letters and are often clever, logical, and interesting. He uses them when possible by weaving them into his stories.

l: Oz stories, The Emerald City of Oz, Author's Note
s: The stories include ideas supplied by children, including directions about Dorothy, Aunt Em, and Uncle Henry. Baum says children love the stories because children have helped create them.

l: the alliance between Baum and children, The Emerald City of Oz, Author's Note
s: Baum is proud of his alliance with children, whose ideas help shape his stories while he tries to please them. He hopes the partnership will continue for a long time.

l: The Emerald City of Oz, The Emerald City of Oz, 1. How the Nome King Became Angry
s: Roquat the Red, the Nome King, is enraged because Dorothy took his Magic Belt, which he believes has reduced his power. His Chief Counselor, Chief Steward Kaliko, and General Blug all fail to satisfy or encourage him, and he orders the Counselor and General thrown away. General Blug explains that the Nomes cannot simply march across the deadly desert to the Land of Oz, so Roquat decides to build a secret tunnel under it and invade the Emerald City. Roquat intends to recover the Belt, destroy Oz and its Emerald City, enslave Princess Ozma and Dorothy, and take revenge, while Ozma and Dorothy do not know he remains a dangerous enemy.

l: Nome King, The Emerald City of Oz, 1. How the Nome King Became Angry
s: Roquat the Red, the Nome King, is angry over losing his Magic Belt and wants to recover it. He orders his Chief Counselor and General Blug thrown away after they frustrate him, then decides to build a tunnel under the deadly desert and invade the Land of Oz.

l: Dorothy, The Emerald City of Oz, 1. How the Nome King Became Angry
s: Dorothy is described as the little girl who captured or took the Nome King's Magic Belt and carried it away. Roquat intends to destroy or enslave her, but she does not know that he remains a dangerous enemy.

l: Ozma, The Emerald City of Oz, 1. How the Nome King Became Angry
s: Princess Ozma rules the Land of Oz and has fairy powers that General Blug says would make the Nome army helpless. Roquat intends to destroy her or enslave her, but she does not know about his plan or that he remains alive under the mountains.

l: Nomes, The Emerald City of Oz, 1. How the Nome King Became Angry
s: The Nomes are subjects of Roquat who live in his underground kingdom and obey his commands. They are miners and are described as good fighters, but General Blug says they are not strong enough to conquer the Emerald City.

l: the Nome King's army, The Emerald City of Oz, 1. How the Nome King Became Angry
s: The Nome army consists of fifty thousand well-drilled Nome soldiers under General Blug. General Blug says the army cannot cross the deadly desert and would be helpless against Princess Ozma's fairy powers, though Roquat plans to send it through a tunnel.

l: the Land of Oz, The Emerald City of Oz, 1. How the Nome King Became Angry
s: The Land of Oz lies beyond the deadly desert and cannot ordinarily be reached by crossing it. Roquat plans to invade it through a secret tunnel, capture it, destroy the Emerald City, and enslave its people.

l: the Emerald City, The Emerald City of Oz, 1. How the Nome King Became Angry
s: The Emerald City is the target of Roquat's planned invasion. He orders General Blug to capture and destroy it, and later decides that a tunnel should lead directly to it.

l: the Deadly Desert, The Emerald City of Oz, 1. How the Nome King Became Angry
s: A deadly desert surrounds the Land of Oz, and no one is able to cross it by ordinary travel. General Blug identifies routes over it through the air or under it through the earth, leading Roquat to choose tunneling.

l: Magic Belt, The Emerald City of Oz, 1. How the Nome King Became Angry
s: The Magic Belt formerly enabled Roquat to carry out many wicked plans and represented half of his power. Dorothy captured it in a fair fight and carried it away, and the Belt is later seen in Ozma's palace by one of Roquat's spies.

l: anger, The Emerald City of Oz, 1. How the Nome King Became Angry
s: Roquat's anger makes him disagreeable and causes everyone, including Kaliko, to avoid him. He says that occasional anger can be enjoyable because it makes others miserable, but constant anger prevents him from taking pleasure in anything else.

l: Magic Belt loss, The Emerald City of Oz, 1. How the Nome King Became Angry
s: The loss of the Magic Belt causes Roquat to become angry because he can no longer perform the magical acts he wants. He believes the loss has taken away half his power and repeatedly insists that he must get the Belt back.

l: capture of the Magic Belt, The Emerald City of Oz, 1. How the Nome King Became Angry
s: The Magic Belt was captured from Roquat after Ozma and her people marched to his underground cavern. The text also says that Dorothy captured it in a fair fight and carried it away, leaving it in the Emerald City with Ozma.

l: Nome King's invasion, The Emerald City of Oz, 1. How the Nome King Became Angry
s: Roquat orders General Blug to march the Nome army to the Land of Oz, capture and destroy the Emerald City, and recover the Magic Belt. Because the army cannot cross the deadly desert or defeat Ozma directly, Roquat plans a secret tunnel under the desert.

l: vengeance against Ozma and her people, The Emerald City of Oz, 1. How the Nome King Became Angry
s: Roquat cannot forgive Dorothy or Princess Ozma for the loss of his Magic Belt and has resolved to take revenge. He intends to destroy the Land of Oz, enslave them and the Oz people, and recover the Belt.

l: The Emerald City of Oz, The Emerald City of Oz, 2. How Uncle Henry Got Into Trouble
s: Dorothy Gale lives with Aunt Em and Uncle Henry on a poor Kansas farm threatened by an unpaid mortgage. The banker gives Uncle Henry thirty days to pay or lose the farm, leaving the older couple afraid they cannot support Dorothy. Dorothy says Ozma can summon her to the Land of Oz, and she plans to go there while finding a way to help her aunt and uncle. At four o’clock, Dorothy makes the secret signal and disappears from her room, leaving Uncle Henry and Aunt Em unable to find her.

l: Dorothy, The Emerald City of Oz, 2. How Uncle Henry Got Into Trouble
s: Dorothy Gale lives on a Kansas farm with Aunt Em and Uncle Henry. She is loving, usually sweet-tempered, and has experienced strange adventures in the Land of Oz. She promises to help her aunt and uncle, then makes a secret signal to Ozma and disappears from her room.

l: Uncle Henry, The Emerald City of Oz, 2. How Uncle Henry Got Into Trouble
s: Uncle Henry is a poor, aging farmer whose health has become too weak for him to work easily. He mortgages his farm after a cyclone destroys his house and later faces losing the farm because he cannot repay the loan. He doubts that Dorothy's fairyland is real and worries that she might be mistreated there.

l: Aunt Em, The Emerald City of Oz, 2. How Uncle Henry Got Into Trouble
s: Aunt Em does the housework with Dorothy's help and worries about the family's poverty. She tells Dorothy that she and Uncle Henry may have to leave the farm and that Dorothy might need to work. Although she is heartbroken at the thought of losing Dorothy, she agrees that Dorothy may be better off living with her fairy friends.

l: Ozma, The Emerald City of Oz, 2. How Uncle Henry Got Into Trouble
s: Ozma is the girl Ruler of the Land of Oz and Dorothy's faithful friend. She has made Dorothy a Princess and has often asked Dorothy to live in the Emerald City. Through her Magic Picture, Ozma sees Dorothy every day at four o'clock and can summon her using the Magic Belt when Dorothy makes the secret sign.

l: the banker, The Emerald City of Oz, 2. How Uncle Henry Got Into Trouble
s: The banker loaned Uncle Henry money and warns him that he must repay it on a certain day or lose his farm. He later gives Uncle Henry thirty days to pay the money.

l: Kansas, The Emerald City of Oz, 2. How Uncle Henry Got Into Trouble
s: Kansas is where Dorothy Gale lives with Aunt Em and Uncle Henry. The family’s farm there suffers from poor crops when rain does not come, contributing to their poverty.

l: Uncle Henry and Aunt Em's farm, The Emerald City of Oz, 2. How Uncle Henry Got Into Trouble
s: The farm is Uncle Henry and Aunt Em's home and means of earning a living. It produces only enough crops to buy food, and it has been mortgaged because Uncle Henry needed money to rebuild after a cyclone. The family must leave it if the mortgage is not paid.

l: the Land of Oz, The Emerald City of Oz, 2. How Uncle Henry Got Into Trouble
s: The Land of Oz is a fairy country that Dorothy has visited several times and described to her aunt and uncle. It contains great riches, unusual people, and the Emerald City. Dorothy plans to return there because Ozma can provide her with a home.

l: the Emerald City, The Emerald City of Oz, 2. How Uncle Henry Got Into Trouble
s: The Emerald City is in the Land of Oz and is ruled by Ozma. Dorothy describes it as a beautiful place where Ozma lives in a palace and where great emeralds are common.

l: the mortgage, The Emerald City of Oz, 2. How Uncle Henry Got Into Trouble
s: The mortgage was taken out by Uncle Henry to pay for rebuilding his house after a cyclone carried the original one away. Because the farm's crops only pay for food, the mortgage cannot be repaid, putting the farm at risk.

l: Uncle Henry's financial trouble, The Emerald City of Oz, 2. How Uncle Henry Got Into Trouble
s: Uncle Henry grows poorer because of failed crops, rebuilding costs, poor health, and the expense of a sea voyage to Australia with Dorothy. The banker demands payment within thirty days or the family must give up the farm. Uncle Henry and Aunt Em fear they will have to leave and that Dorothy may need to work.

l: Dorothy's disappearance to Oz, The Emerald City of Oz, 2. How Uncle Henry Got Into Trouble
s: Dorothy goes to her attic room with Toto and waits until four o'clock, when she makes the secret signal agreed upon with Ozma. Uncle Henry and Aunt Em wait downstairs, but after hearing no sound they find that the room is empty.

l: The Emerald City of Oz, The Emerald City of Oz, 3. How Ozma Granted Dorothy's Request
s: Dorothy Gale asks Ozma to let Uncle Henry and Aunt Em leave their failing Kansas farm and live with her in the Land of Oz. Ozma agrees to give them a comfortable place in Oz and invites Dorothy to live in the palace as her constant companion. Because Uncle Henry and Aunt Em may not believe in Oz and could become nervous, Ozma plans to transport them without warning using the Magic Belt. Their arrival is planned for the next morning, after rooms are prepared in the Emerald City of Oz.

l: Dorothy, The Emerald City of Oz, 3. How Ozma Granted Dorothy's Request
s: Dorothy Gale tells Ozma that Uncle Henry and Aunt Em are in serious trouble because they are about to lose their Kansas farm. She asks to live in the Land of Oz with them, and Ozma agrees to bring them there. Ozma also tells Dorothy that she will live in her own rooms in the palace as Ozma's constant companion.

l: Ozma, The Emerald City of Oz, 3. How Ozma Granted Dorothy's Request
s: Ozma listens sympathetically to Dorothy's request and agrees to invite Uncle Henry and Aunt Em to live in the Land of Oz. She plans to provide them with a comfortable place where they need not work more than they wish. Ozma decides to use the Magic Belt to transport them to the Emerald City of Oz without warning them.

l: Uncle Henry, The Emerald City of Oz, 3. How Ozma Granted Dorothy's Request
s: Uncle Henry is poor because his Kansas farm does not produce enough, and he borrowed money against it. Since he cannot repay the loan, his farm is going to be taken, leaving him without a home. Ozma agrees to bring him to the Land of Oz, where he can live comfortably and need not work more than he chooses.

l: Aunt Em, The Emerald City of Oz, 3. How Ozma Granted Dorothy's Request
s: Aunt Em is facing the loss of her Kansas home with Uncle Henry. Dorothy says that she and Uncle Henry are too old to do much hard work, so Ozma agrees to bring Aunt Em to the Land of Oz and provide a comfortable place for her.

l: Oz, The Emerald City of Oz, 3. How Ozma Granted Dorothy's Request
s: The Land of Oz is described as a prosperous fairyland ruled by Ozma, with no disease, poverty, or money and with work and resources shared among its inhabitants. Its people are peaceful, kind, and happy, although remote areas contain dangers such as Hammer-Heads, Kalidahs, and Fighting Trees. Ozma agrees to admit Uncle Henry and Aunt Em so Dorothy can live there with them.

l: the Emerald City, The Emerald City of Oz, 3. How Ozma Granted Dorothy's Request
s: The Emerald City of Oz is the capital of the Land of Oz and is built from beautiful marbles decorated with large emeralds and other jewels. Ozma's palace is located there, and Dorothy is transported to it after making a secret signal. Ozma plans to bring Uncle Henry and Aunt Em to the Emerald City after rooms have been prepared for them.

l: Kansas, The Emerald City of Oz, 3. How Ozma Granted Dorothy's Request
s: Kansas is where Uncle Henry and Aunt Em live on a farm that does not produce enough money to support them. Because Uncle Henry cannot repay borrowed money, the farm is going to be taken, and Dorothy concludes that they cannot remain there safely.

l: Uncle Henry and Aunt Em's farm, The Emerald City of Oz, 3. How Ozma Granted Dorothy's Request
s: Uncle Henry and Aunt Em's farm in Kansas is insufficiently profitable, and Uncle Henry has pledged it as repayment for a loan. Since he cannot repay the money, the farm is going to be taken, leaving them without a place to live.

l: the request to bring Uncle Henry and Aunt Em to Oz, The Emerald City of Oz, 3. How Ozma Granted Dorothy's Request
s: Dorothy's request is that Ozma bring Uncle Henry and Aunt Em to the Land of Oz so Dorothy can live there with them. Ozma gladly grants the request and promises to find them a comfortable home while allowing Dorothy to remain her companion.

l: the transport of Uncle Henry and Aunt Em to Oz, The Emerald City of Oz, 3. How Ozma Granted Dorothy's Request
s: Ozma plans to transport Uncle Henry and Aunt Em to the Emerald City without warning them first. She believes this will prevent them from becoming nervous if they are told they are making a magical journey, and she plans to carry it out the next morning.

l: Magic Belt, The Emerald City of Oz, 3. How Ozma Granted Dorothy's Request
s: Ozma intends to use the Magic Belt to transport Uncle Henry and Aunt Em from Kansas to the Emerald City of Oz. She plans to obtain it after breakfast and use it to bring them to the palace, where Dorothy can explain their new surroundings.

l: The Emerald City of Oz, The Emerald City of Oz, 4. How The Nome King Planned Revenge
s: King Roquat the Red plans to conquer the Land of Oz, destroy the Emerald City, enslave its people, and recover his Magic Belt. He appoints Guph as General after General Crinkle refuses the mission and is taken to the torture chamber. Guph warns that Oz's magic powers make a direct attack impossible and proposes gathering evil creatures as allies. The Nome King orders Guph to arrange this alliance while he begins digging an underground tunnel to Oz.

l: Nome King, The Emerald City of Oz, 4. How The Nome King Planned Revenge
s: King Roquat the Red plans to conquer the Land of Oz, destroy the Emerald City, enslave its people, and recover his Magic Belt. He appoints Guph as General and orders him to obtain allies among evil powers while the King begins digging a tunnel to Oz.

l: General Guph, The Emerald City of Oz, 4. How The Nome King Planned Revenge
s: Guph, an old Nome, volunteers to become General because he hates good, happy, contented, and prosperous people. He tells King Roquat that Oz cannot be conquered without additional magic power and proposes forming an alliance with evil creatures. He is ordered to visit the Chief of the Whimsies and arrange assistance.

l: Dorothy, The Emerald City of Oz, 4. How The Nome King Planned Revenge
s: Dorothy is said to possess the Nome King's Magic Belt. Guph identifies her possession of the Belt as one of the magical obstacles to conquering Oz.

l: Ozma, The Emerald City of Oz, 4. How The Nome King Planned Revenge
s: Ozma is the Princess who rules Oz and possesses a fairy wand. Guph says that King Roquat and the Nomes would have no chance against her without additional magical power.

l: Nomes, The Emerald City of Oz, 4. How The Nome King Planned Revenge
s: The Nomes are immortal creatures who work as metal workers and miners when they are not soldiers. They are physically strong but, according to Guph, are not strong in magic.

l: the Nome King's army, The Emerald City of Oz, 4. How The Nome King Planned Revenge
s: The Nome army consists of fifty thousand Nomes armed with swords and pikes. It is well drilled and wears rock-colored uniforms, but Guph says it lacks the magical strength needed to defeat Oz.

l: the Land of Oz, The Emerald City of Oz, 4. How The Nome King Planned Revenge
s: The Land of Oz is described as a powerful fairy country ruled by Ozma. King Roquat plans to conquer it, while Guph seeks evil allies to help overcome its magical defenses.

l: the Emerald City, The Emerald City of Oz, 4. How The Nome King Planned Revenge
s: The Emerald City is the target of the Nome King's planned attack. He orders his General to conquer its people, destroy the city, and take its gold, silver, and precious stones.

l: Magic Belt, The Emerald City of Oz, 4. How The Nome King Planned Revenge
s: The Magic Belt was lost by King Roquat and is now possessed by Dorothy. The Nome King orders Guph's army to recapture it and return it to him.

l: Nome King's tunnel, The Emerald City of Oz, 4. How The Nome King Planned Revenge
s: King Roquat plans to bore an underground tunnel from the Nome kingdom to the Emerald City. He says he will begin digging it while Guph makes arrangements with evil powers.

l: evil spirits, The Emerald City of Oz, 4. How The Nome King Planned Revenge
s: Guph says that certain evil creatures possess enough magic to destroy and conquer the Land of Oz. He plans to obtain their assistance and band them together against Oz.

l: Nome King's invasion, The Emerald City of Oz, 4. How The Nome King Planned Revenge
s: The planned conquest involves marching the Nome army through a tunnel, conquering and destroying the Oz people and the Emerald City, taking its treasures, enslaving its people, and recovering the Magic Belt. Guph intends to use surprise and allied evil powers to make the conquest possible.

l: sorcery, The Emerald City of Oz, 4. How The Nome King Planned Revenge
s: Magic is presented as the chief defense of Oz. Ozma has a fairy wand, Glinda the Good commands the spirits of the air, and a wonderful Wizard lives in Ozma's palace; Guph says the Nomes cannot defeat these powers without help.

l: Oz people, The Emerald City of Oz, 4. How The Nome King Planned Revenge
s: The Oz people are described by King Roquat as good, happy, contented, and prosperous. They are the intended victims of the Nome King's plan to conquer, destroy, and enslave them.

l: the planned alliance against Oz, The Emerald City of Oz, 4. How The Nome King Planned Revenge
s: Guph plans to unite evil creatures with sufficient magical power to attack Oz. He believes that this alliance will allow the Nomes to surprise and defeat Ozma and her people.

l: The Emerald City of Oz, The Emerald City of Oz, 5. How Dorothy Became a Princess
s: Dorothy returns to the Emerald City, where the people warmly welcome her and Princess Ozma declares that she must assume her rightful rank as a Princess of Oz. Ozma uses the Magic Belt to transport Dorothy's Uncle Henry and Aunt Em from Kansas to the Emerald City. Although they arrive in their work clothes and are startled by the palace and its creatures, Ozma welcomes them as honored subjects and gives them a permanent home in the Land of Oz. Dorothy is delighted that her relatives will share in the happiness and comforts of Oz.

l: Dorothy, The Emerald City of Oz, 5. How Dorothy Became a Princess
s: Dorothy receives a joyful welcome in the Emerald City because the people consider her a favorite and believe she has brought them good luck. Princess Ozma appoints her a Princess of Oz, and Dorothy dresses in a sky-blue silk gown, pearl-trimmed shoes, and a pearl coronet. She is especially happy that Uncle Henry and Aunt Em are brought to Oz to live with her.

l: Ozma, The Emerald City of Oz, 5. How Dorothy Became a Princess
s: Princess Ozma welcomes Dorothy back and tells her to assume her rightful rank as a Princess of Oz. She uses the Magic Belt to bring Uncle Henry and Aunt Em from Kansas, receives them graciously in the Throne Room, and asks the people of Oz to show them kindness and honor.

l: Uncle Henry, The Emerald City of Oz, 5. How Dorothy Became a Princess
s: Uncle Henry is transported from his barn in Kansas to the Throne Room in the Emerald City while wearing work clothes. He is startled by the palace and the animals, but Dorothy reassures him that he will live comfortably and happily in Oz without having to work until his back aches.

l: Aunt Em, The Emerald City of Oz, 5. How Dorothy Became a Princess
s: Aunt Em is transported from her household work in Kansas to the Throne Room while wearing a calico dress, apron, and Uncle Henry's slippers. She is frightened and confused by the sudden change, but Princess Ozma welcomes her as an honored subject and Dorothy tells her she will live comfortably in Oz.

l: the Emerald City, The Emerald City of Oz, 5. How Dorothy Became a Princess
s: The Emerald City gives Dorothy a joyful welcome when she returns. Its palace contains rooms reserved for Dorothy, a magnificent Throne Room, a golden throne, court members, the Cowardly Lion, the Hungry Tiger, music, and colored perfumed fountains.

l: the Land of Oz, The Emerald City of Oz, 5. How Dorothy Became a Princess
s: The Land of Oz regards Dorothy as an important and beloved person because of the good she has done there. It becomes the permanent home of Dorothy, Uncle Henry, and Aunt Em, who are told that they now belong to it.

l: Magic Belt, The Emerald City of Oz, 5. How Dorothy Became a Princess
s: The Magic Belt is worn by Princess Ozma and is used to transport Uncle Henry and Aunt Em from Kansas to the Emerald City.

l: Dorothy's appointment as a Princess of Oz, The Emerald City of Oz, 5. How Dorothy Became a Princess
s: Princess Ozma declares that Dorothy must assume her rightful rank as a Princess of Oz and dress in a manner suited to that position. Dorothy accepts the appointment while remaining a simple and unaffected little girl.

l: the transport of Uncle Henry and Aunt Em to Oz, The Emerald City of Oz, 5. How Dorothy Became a Princess
s: Princess Ozma uses the Magic Belt to transport Uncle Henry and Aunt Em from Kansas to the Throne Room in the Emerald City. They arrive suddenly and unprepared, but Ozma welcomes them and arranges for them to live permanently in Oz.

l: The Emerald City of Oz, The Emerald City of Oz, 6. How Guph Visited the Whimsies
s: General Guph, the new General of the Nome King's army, plans carefully to help the Nomes conquer the Land of Oz. Roquat the Red orders a large tunnel built beneath the desert from the Nome country toward the Emerald City so the Nome army can attack by surprise. Guph visits the Whimsies and promises that the Nome King will give them large natural heads if they help fight for him. The Whimsies accept the bargain and agree to join the Nome conquest of Oz.

l: General Guph, The Emerald City of Oz, 6. How Guph Visited the Whimsies
s: General Guph becomes the new General of the Nome King's army and accepts the position because he wants to spread unhappiness and conquer Oz. He visits the Whimsies, promises them a reward for helping the Nomes, and successfully gains them as allies.

l: Nome King, The Emerald City of Oz, 6. How Guph Visited the Whimsies
s: Roquat the Red plans to conquer Oz and recover his Magic Belt. He orders a thousand miners to begin building a broad tunnel beneath the desert toward the Emerald City.

l: Nomes, The Emerald City of Oz, 6. How Guph Visited the Whimsies
s: The Nomes live in underground caverns and are experienced at making tunnels. They begin tunneling beneath the desert and seek the Whimsies' help in conquering Oz.

l: the Nome King's army, The Emerald City of Oz, 6. How Guph Visited the Whimsies
s: The Nome King's army is led by General Guph in the planned invasion of Oz. Roquat intends for the army to march through the tunnel and emerge in the Emerald City without warning.

l: the Land of Oz, The Emerald City of Oz, 6. How Guph Visited the Whimsies
s: The Land of Oz is the target of the Nome King's planned surprise attack. Roquat intends to conquer and plunder it, destroy the country, and capture its people before they can prepare a defense.

l: Nome King's tunnel, The Emerald City of Oz, 6. How Guph Visited the Whimsies
s: The tunnel is being built beneath the desert from the Nome King's mountains toward the Emerald City. It is designed to be high and broad enough for the Nome army to pass through and emerge without warning.

l: Whimsies, The Emerald City of Oz, 6. How Guph Visited the Whimsies
s: The Whimsies are strong, muscular evil spirits with tiny natural heads covered by large pasteboard heads, and they cannot be killed. They agree to fight for the Nome King after Guph promises that their natural heads will be enlarged if the Nomes capture the Magic Belt.

l: Chief of the Whimsies, The Emerald City of Oz, 6. How Guph Visited the Whimsies
s: The Chief of the Whimsies is no wiser or more capable than the others and was chosen because no Whimsie was better suited to rule. After hearing Guph's offer, he consults his people, who agree to help the Nomes.

l: Magic Belt, The Emerald City of Oz, 6. How Guph Visited the Whimsies
s: The Magic Belt is described by Guph as belonging to the Nome King and having been stolen from him by the Oz people. Guph promises that Roquat will use its power to give the Whimsies large natural heads if they help capture it.

l: Nome King's invasion, The Emerald City of Oz, 6. How Guph Visited the Whimsies
s: The Nome conquest of Oz is planned as a surprise invasion through a tunnel reaching the Emerald City. General Guph recruits the Whimsies as powerful allies by promising them a reward for fighting.

l: The Emerald City of Oz, The Emerald City of Oz, 7. How Aunt Em Conquered the Lion
s: Dorothy shows Aunt Em and Uncle Henry their luxurious rooms in Ozma's palace and introduces them to the palace and its inhabitants. They visit Billina, who explains that her large chicken family lives safely and comfortably in the Land of Oz. While exploring the palace grounds, Aunt Em and Uncle Henry encounter the Cowardly Lion and frighten him with Aunt Em's fierce gaze. The Lion explains that he is Dorothy's friend, serves Ozma as a body guard, and remains frightened despite winning his battles.

l: Dorothy, The Emerald City of Oz, 7. How Aunt Em Conquered the Lion
s: Dorothy shows Aunt Em and Uncle Henry their rooms, the palace, and the surrounding grounds. She introduces them to Billina and explains where several of her friends live. She leaves Aunt Em and Uncle Henry to explore while she stays with Billina's young chickens.

l: Aunt Em, The Emerald City of Oz, 7. How Aunt Em Conquered the Lion
s: Aunt Em is given luxurious rooms, fine clothing, and gold toilet articles in the palace, although she feels the finery is too grand for her. She visits Billina's chicken family with Dorothy and is impressed by the talking chickens. When she and Uncle Henry encounter the Lion, she tries to conquer him with her fierce gaze and succeeds in frightening him.

l: Uncle Henry, The Emerald City of Oz, 7. How Aunt Em Conquered the Lion
s: Uncle Henry accepts his new palace accommodations and clothing calmly, choosing a blue satin suit and refusing assistance from a servant. He explores the grounds with Aunt Em and helps recognize the Lion as Dorothy's friend. He explains that the Lion is the Cowardly Lion because he speaks meekly and looks ashamed.

l: Ozma, The Emerald City of Oz, 7. How Aunt Em Conquered the Lion
s: Ozma requires Aunt Em and Uncle Henry to live in the palace and has royal dressmakers prepare clothing for Aunt Em. She provides for the people and animals in the Land of Oz, including Billina's chickens, and has the Cowardly Lion and the Hungry Tiger serve as her body guards.

l: the Land of Oz, The Emerald City of Oz, 7. How Aunt Em Conquered the Lion
s: The Land of Oz becomes Aunt Em and Uncle Henry's permanent home. They find it beautiful, safe, and more delightful than any place they have known, and they are treated with respect and consideration.

l: Ozma's palace, The Emerald City of Oz, 7. How Aunt Em Conquered the Lion
s: The palace provides luxurious rooms, fine furnishings, clothing, bathrooms, gardens, and grounds for Aunt Em and Uncle Henry. Its grounds are enclosed by a high wall of green marble set with emeralds, so Dorothy knows they cannot get lost.

l: Billina, The Emerald City of Oz, 7. How Aunt Em Conquered the Lion
s: Billina welcomes Dorothy, Aunt Em, and Uncle Henry and shows them her house and her chicken family. She is the acknowledged Queen and Governor of every chicken in Oz and has nine living hens named Dorothys and two roosters named Daniels. Her chickens are protected, well supplied, and taught good manners and grammar.

l: the Cowardly Lion, The Emerald City of Oz, 7. How Aunt Em Conquered the Lion
s: The Cowardly Lion encounters Aunt Em and Uncle Henry on the palace grounds and is frightened by Aunt Em's fierce stare. He identifies himself as Dorothy's old chum, the King of Beasts, and one of Ozma's body guards. He says that he trembles with fear in battle but fights hard and has always won.

l: the human eye, The Emerald City of Oz, 7. How Aunt Em Conquered the Lion
s: Aunt Em believes that savage beasts can be conquered by the human eye. Her fierce and penetrating gaze frightens the Lion, who calls the human eye a fearful weapon.

l: The Emerald City of Oz, The Emerald City of Oz, 8. How the Grand Gallipoot Joined The Nomes
s: Guph crosses the Ripple Land and reaches the domain of the Growleywogs, where the Grand Gallipoot hears his proposal to help the Nomes conquer the Land of Oz. The Growleywogs agree to provide eighteen thousand warriors in exchange for twenty thousand people of Oz as slaves, while secretly planning to conquer the Nomes afterward. Guph is imprisoned and tortured before being released with the promise of assistance. Having secured the Whimsies and Growleywogs as allies, he decides to seek still more powerful support.

l: General Guph, The Emerald City of Oz, 8. How the Grand Gallipoot Joined The Nomes
s: Guph crosses the changing hills and valleys of the Ripple Land and reaches the Growleywogs' domain. He persuades the Grand Gallipoot to promise assistance in conquering the Land of Oz, despite being tossed into the air, imprisoned, stuck with pins, and having his whiskers pulled out. He leaves delighted with the promise and begins seeking still more allies.

l: Whimsies, The Emerald City of Oz, 8. How the Grand Gallipoot Joined The Nomes
s: The Whimsies are identified as allies whose assistance Guph has already secured before reaching the Growleywogs.

l: Growleywogs, The Emerald City of Oz, 8. How the Grand Gallipoot Joined The Nomes
s: The Growleywogs are gigantic, extremely strong creatures made of bone, skin, and muscle, and they are described as surly, unsociable, and hated by others. They agree to help the Nomes conquer the Land of Oz in return for twenty thousand people of Oz as slaves, while secretly intending to conquer the Nomes afterward.

l: Grand Gallipoot, The Emerald City of Oz, 8. How the Grand Gallipoot Joined The Nomes
s: The Grand Gallipoot questions Guph about the proposed conquest and agrees that the Growleywogs will assist the Nomes. He promises to march with eighteen thousand powerful warriors, while privately planning to take the Magic Belt, enslave the Nome King, and seize Oz's people and treasure.

l: Nome King, The Emerald City of Oz, 8. How the Grand Gallipoot Joined The Nomes
s: Nome King Roquat the Red sends Guph to seek the Growleywogs' assistance in conquering the Land of Oz. The Growleywogs secretly plan to conquer the Nomes after Oz is defeated and make Roquat their slave.

l: Nomes, The Emerald City of Oz, 8. How the Grand Gallipoot Joined The Nomes
s: The Nomes are preparing to invade the Land of Oz and seek the Growleywogs' aid because they need powerful assistance to avoid defeat. The Growleywogs agree to help them but secretly intend to conquer them afterward.

l: the Land of Oz, The Emerald City of Oz, 8. How the Grand Gallipoot Joined The Nomes
s: The Land of Oz is described as a happy, contented land ruled by Ozma, and the Nomes and Growleywogs plan to conquer and destroy it. The Growleywogs expect to take its people, gold, jewels, and notable inhabitants as slaves or possessions.

l: Ozma, The Emerald City of Oz, 8. How the Grand Gallipoot Joined The Nomes
s: Ozma is described by Guph as a kind and good ruler of the Land of Oz. She previously marched against the Nomes with an army after they enslaved the Royal Family of Ev.

l: the Emerald City, The Emerald City of Oz, 8. How the Grand Gallipoot Joined The Nomes
s: The Emerald City is the intended target of the Nome invasion. Guph says the Nomes and their allies plan to reach it through a tunnel and destroy it.

l: Magic Belt, The Emerald City of Oz, 8. How the Grand Gallipoot Joined The Nomes
s: The Magic Belt was taken from the Nome King by Ozma, Dorothy, and their companions after they entered the Nome King's cavern and freed the slaves from Ev. The Growleywogs plan to seize the belt after helping conquer Oz.

l: Nome King's tunnel, The Emerald City of Oz, 8. How the Grand Gallipoot Joined The Nomes
s: The Nome King is building a tunnel under the deadly desert so that the Nomes and their allies can march into the Land of Oz and reach the Emerald City.

l: Growleywog warriors, The Emerald City of Oz, 8. How the Grand Gallipoot Joined The Nomes
s: The Grand Gallipoot promises to march with eighteen thousand of his most powerful Growleywog warriors to assist the Nomes in conquering the Land of Oz.

l: Nome King's invasion, The Emerald City of Oz, 8. How the Grand Gallipoot Joined The Nomes
s: The proposed conquest is organized by the Nomes with help from the Growleywogs and a tunnel under the deadly desert. The Growleywogs expect to destroy Ozma's domain, enslave twenty thousand people of Oz, and take its treasure, while Guph hopes the victory will increase his own power.

l: Growleywog assistance to the Nomes, The Emerald City of Oz, 8. How the Grand Gallipoot Joined The Nomes
s: The Growleywogs agree to assist the Nomes in conquering the Land of Oz, promising eighteen thousand warriors. In exchange, they are promised twenty thousand people of Oz as slaves, though they secretly intend to conquer the Nomes after the campaign.

l: The Emerald City of Oz, The Emerald City of Oz, 9. How the Wogglebug Taught Athletics
s: Dorothy asks Ozma to find work for Uncle Henry and Aunt Em, so Ozma sends them on a journey through the Land of Oz with Dorothy and an escort. The party travels in a red wagon drawn by the wooden Sawhorse and visits the Royal Athletic College of Oz, directed by Professor H. M. Wogglebug, T.E. The college emphasizes sports, while students use the Wizard's School Pills to learn subjects such as algebra, geography, Latin, grammar, and spelling without ordinary study. After meeting the Wogglebug and seeing the college, the travelers continue their journey.

l: Dorothy, The Emerald City of Oz, 9. How the Wogglebug Taught Athletics
s: Dorothy settles into her new home in the Emerald City and becomes concerned that Uncle Henry and Aunt Em have no work to occupy them. She asks Ozma for help and then leads her relatives and their escort on a journey through the Land of Oz. At the Royal Athletic College of Oz, she questions when the students study and how they take the School Pills.

l: Uncle Henry, The Emerald City of Oz, 9. How the Wogglebug Taught Athletics
s: Uncle Henry feels restless because he has no work to do in Oz, and Billina scolds him when he feeds the chickens between meals. He joins Dorothy's journey through the Land of Oz and is astonished that the wooden Sawhorse can think and speak. He says that he likes Oz better than Kansas and admires the Sawhorse.

l: Aunt Em, The Emerald City of Oz, 9. How the Wogglebug Taught Athletics
s: Aunt Em is unhappy that she cannot do household work and finds constant finery and leisure difficult. She travels with Dorothy and the others, enjoys the impressive departure, and says that the Love Magnet might have helped her family in Kansas. At the Royal Athletic College of Oz, she compares the School Pills to taking medicine.

l: Ozma, The Emerald City of Oz, 9. How the Wogglebug Taught Athletics
s: Ozma notices that Uncle Henry and Aunt Em are uneasy without light tasks and proposes that Dorothy take them on a journey while she searches for suitable occupations. She provides an escort and prepares the party to leave the next morning.

l: the Emerald City, The Emerald City of Oz, 9. How the Wogglebug Taught Athletics
s: The Emerald City is Dorothy's new home, where Uncle Henry and Aunt Em are treated courteously but struggle to adjust to palace life. The travelers leave the city through its great wall and are cheered by the people as they depart.

l: Oz, The Emerald City of Oz, 9. How the Wogglebug Taught Athletics
s: Oz has a Royal Athletic College where young Ozites practice many sports and use School Pills for academic subjects. Uncle Henry says that he prefers Oz to Kansas.

l: Wizard, The Emerald City of Oz, 9. How the Wogglebug Taught Athletics
s: The Wizard joins Dorothy's party with the Shaggy Man and helps guide the Sawhorse. He invented the School Pills and explains that one accidentally taught a chicken to recite poems after it swallowed an Elocution Pill.

l: the Shaggy Man, The Emerald City of Oz, 9. How the Wogglebug Taught Athletics
s: The Shaggy Man joins the journey and rides in the third seat of the wagon. He explains that the Love Magnet hangs above the Emerald City's gateway and asks the Sawhorse to slow down so the passengers can enjoy the scenery.

l: Omby Amby, The Emerald City of Oz, 9. How the Wogglebug Taught Athletics
s: Omby Amby, the Captain General of Ozma's army, accompanies Dorothy's party. He is described as tall, slim, gentle, and dressed in a gay uniform. At the college, he approves of the School Pills because studying arithmetic once gave him headaches.

l: Sawhorse, The Emerald City of Oz, 9. How the Wogglebug Taught Athletics
s: The Sawhorse draws the party's red wagon through the Land of Oz. It can travel extremely fast, but slows down when asked so the passengers can admire the scenery. The Wizard says that sawdust brains made from hard knots allow the Sawhorse to think through knotty problems.

l: Professor Wogglebug's Athletic College, The Emerald City of Oz, 9. How the Wogglebug Taught Athletics
s: The Royal Athletic College of Oz stands on a green plain and is directed by Professor H. M. Wogglebug, T.E. Its students spend their class hours playing football, baseball, tennis, golf, swimming, rowing, basketball, cricket, boxing, and wrestling. The college uses School Pills so students can acquire academic knowledge without interrupting their athletic activities.

l: Professor H. M. Wogglebug, T.E., The Emerald City of Oz, 9. How the Wogglebug Taught Athletics
s: Professor H. M. Wogglebug, T.E., welcomes Dorothy and her companions to the Royal Athletic College of Oz. He proudly explains that the college teaches scientific college athletics and uses School Pills for subjects including algebra, geography, Latin, grammar, spelling, mathematics, and literature. He considers the pills a successful way to save time for athletic practice.

l: college athletics, The Emerald City of Oz, 9. How the Wogglebug Taught Athletics
s: College athletics at the Royal Athletic College of Oz includes football, baseball, tennis, golf, swimming, rowing, basketball, cricket, boxing, and wrestling. The students devote most of their time to these activities because the School Pills replace much of their ordinary study.

l: the Wizard's School Pills, The Emerald City of Oz, 9. How the Wogglebug Taught Athletics
s: The School Pills are invented by the Wizard and are used to teach academic subjects without lengthy study. Different pills cover algebra, geography, Latin, grammar, spelling, and elocution, with instructions for when to take them. The Wogglebug says they let students spend more time practicing athletics.

l: the travelers' journey, The Emerald City of Oz, 9. How the Wogglebug Taught Athletics
s: The journey through the Land of Oz is arranged by Ozma so Dorothy can take Uncle Henry and Aunt Em away from their restless palace life. Dorothy, her relatives, the Wizard, the Shaggy Man, Omby Amby, Toto, and Billina travel in a red wagon drawn by the Sawhorse. Their first described stop is the Royal Athletic College of Oz, after which they continue their journey.

l: The Emerald City of Oz, The Emerald City of Oz, 10. How the Cuttenclips Lived
s: Dorothy, the Wizard, the Shaggy Man, and their traveling party visit the Cuttenclips, a village of living paper dolls ruled by Miss Cuttenclip. Miss Cuttenclip explains that Glinda gave her magic live paper, which makes the dolls she cuts out alive and able to think and talk. The visitors observe the village and its delicate inhabitants, but the Shaggy Man’s sneeze blows many paper dolls over and damages two houses. The party leaves after helping restore the dolls, while Miss Cuttenclip warns that visitors must avoid making breezes.

l: Dorothy, The Emerald City of Oz, 10. How the Cuttenclips Lived
s: Dorothy travels with the party to the Cuttenclip village and explains that the Cuttenclips are living paper dolls. She carefully helps stand up the paper soldiers and later helps Miss Cuttenclip rescue the dolls scattered by the Shaggy Man’s sneeze.

l: Wizard, The Emerald City of Oz, 10. How the Cuttenclips Lived
s: The Wizard travels with the party to the Cuttenclip village. He jokes that the Cuttenclips are flimsy, accidentally blows over the line of paper soldiers by letting the door swing, and gently removes a paper boy from a tree after Billina knocks him there.

l: the Shaggy Man, The Emerald City of Oz, 10. How the Cuttenclips Lived
s: The Shaggy Man visits the Cuttenclip village with the party. His powerful sneeze blows down dozens of paper dolls, scatters and wrinkles them, and contributes to two cardboard houses tumbling over; he is ashamed and helps with the rescue.

l: Miss Cuttenclip, The Emerald City of Oz, 10. How the Cuttenclips Lived
s: Miss Cuttenclip is the flesh-and-blood Queen of the Cuttenclip village and the maker of its paper people, houses, trees, and flowers. She received magic paper from Glinda, does not grow older, and remains happy making her village.
